bib.title: Personalization of Large Language Models: A Survey
bib.venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), accepted; arXiv v3 13 Jul 2025

read.skipped: Reference list (about 1200 lines) skimmed for arXiv ids only; body, tables and conclusion read in full. No appendix exists.

question: How can the two separate lines of work on personalized LLMs (personalized text generation and downstream-task personalization such as recommendation) be unified under one taxonomy of granularity, techniques, metrics, datasets and applications?
hypothesis: The two directions are not fundamentally distinct and will converge into unified systems; a shared formalization lets them share datasets, techniques and evaluation.
contributions: A unifying view and taxonomy for the usage of personalized LLMs: direct text generation vs indirect downstream task (Sec 2)
A taxonomy of personalization granularity: user-level, persona-level, global preference (Sec 4)
A taxonomy of techniques: RAG, prompting, representation learning, RLHF (Sec 5)
A taxonomy of metrics and evaluation: intrinsic vs extrinsic (Sec 6)
A taxonomy of datasets: with and without ground-truth user text (Sec 7)
Open problems: evaluation, cold start, bias, privacy, multimodality (Sec 9)

results.claim: Richardson et al. report that combining BM25 retrieval with LLM-generated user summaries improved LaMP performance while retrieving 75% less user data.
results.source: Richardson et al. (2023), Integrating summarization and retrieval for enhanced personalization via large language models, arXiv:2310.20081
results.setup: LaMP benchmark tasks; BM25 retrieval plus task-aware LLM user summaries in the prompt (Sec 5.1.1)
results.quote: achieving improved performance on LaMP tasks while reducing the volume of retrieved data by 75%.
results.note: Survey gives no baseline or metric values for the underlying paper.

results.claim: Kang et al. find LLMs underperform traditional recommenders zero-shot but match or beat them when fine-tuned on minimal interaction data, and models of 100B+ parameters do better and converge faster.
results.source: Kang et al. (2023), cited in Sec 5.2.1
results.setup: User rating prediction from past rating history and candidate item features, zero-shot and few-shot prompting plus fine-tuning (Sec 5.2.1)

results.claim: Dense retrievers generally beat sparse retrievers on downstream personalization but need task training, which costs more.
results.setup: Survey judgement across LaMP-style personalization work (Sec 5.1.2); no numbers given

results.claim: Prompt-based personalization is flexible with moderate user data but degrades as the context window saturates; fine-tuning or user embeddings give deeper gains but overfit when per-user data is sparse.
results.source: Kumar et al. (2024) LongLaMP and Salemi et al. (2023) LaMP, as summarised in Sec 5.5
results.setup: LaMP and LongLaMP benchmarks; FLAN-T5 fine-tuning, user embeddings, retrieval (BM25, Contriever)

limits: Survey only: no experiments, no method comparison with shared numbers; effectiveness statements in Sec 5.5 are qualitative and rest on LaMP/LongLaMP.
Authors concede no comprehensive quantitative metric exists for degree of personalization; existing metrics are task-specific and mostly do not measure personalization directly (Sec 9.1).
No LLM-as-a-judge framework for personalization exists to their knowledge; judges risk persona injection, self-favouring, positional bias, instability (Sec 6.1, 9.1).
Cold start is under-studied: many datasets drop users with fewer than five interactions (Sec 9.2, 4.1).
Black-box retrieval via search APIs is excluded from the survey (Sec 5.1).
Global-preference personalization is covered only for completeness (footnote 1).
The word 'memory' appears only in application examples (MaLP dual-process memory, CoPS sensory/working/long-term memory); there is no treatment of agent memory stores, write policies or forgetting.
Cutoff is mid-2024 for most cited work; dated on fast-moving agent-memory systems.
practices: Choose the technique by constraints: RAG for large or dynamic user profiles that must be retrieved on the fly (Sec 5.5).
Use prompting for conversational systems that can fit brief interaction history without retraining (Sec 5.5).
Use representation learning (fine-tuning, PEFT, user embeddings) when high-quality per-user data and compute are abundant and nuanced personalization matters (Sec 5.5).
Use RLHF-style methods when continuous alignment with user feedback is needed and pairwise preference data is available (Sec 5.5).
Combine sparse (BM25) and dense retrieval to balance efficiency and semantic match (Sec 5.5).
Because user profiles exceed context limits and contain irrelevant text that distracts the model, retrieve or summarize rather than paste the whole history (Sec 5.1, 5.2.3).
Augment sparse or incomplete profiles with LLM-generated summaries or distilled personas (profile-augmented prompting) (Sec 5.2.3).

Use a hierarchy: user-level for frequent users, persona-level for occasional users, global preferences for new users; start persona-level and move to user-level as data accrues to handle cold start (Sec 4.4).
Reduce latency with distillation, caching pipelines, on-demand personalization for high-value users, and federated or on-device personalization (Sec 5.5).
Keep user data accurate and up to date; stale attributes (for example an old job title) are a named failure (Sec 3.5).
Do not rely on interaction history alone, since past interactions may not reflect current preferences (Sec 3.3.2).
Evaluate directly with ROUGE/METEOR against user-written text where it exists, and use human evaluation alongside any LLM judge (Sec 6.1).
Anonymize demographic data and protect PII at data processing, training and retrieval stages (Sec 3.3.1, 9.4).

terms.definition: the process of tailoring a system's output to meet the individual preferences, needs, and characteristics of an individual user or a group of users
the collection of texts and writings generated by a user u (reviews, comments, social media posts)
static characteristics and demographic information associated with a user, such as age, gender, location, occupation, that remain relatively constant over time
dynamic behaviors and activities of a user within a system: clicks, views, purchases and other engagement data
the level of detail at which personalization objectives are defined: individual users, groups of users with a shared persona, or the general public
focuses on the unique preferences and behaviors of a single user, often identified through a user ID; finest granularity, needs enough user data
targets groups of users who share similar characteristics or preferences, represented by a natural-language description
general preferences and norms widely accepted by the general public, used via RLHF
integrates user-specific information into generation: y_hat = M(phi_p(x, A(phi_q(x), D_u, k))); a retrieval module is an example
direct: evaluate the personalized text itself; indirect: use generated text or embeddings to improve a downstream task such as recommendation
intrinsic scores generated text against user-written ground truth; extrinsic scores the downstream application with task metrics
directly including past user history in the prompt
specifying a persona (demographic, character or individualized) in the prompt so the LLM role-plays it
prompting strategies that enrich user history using the LLM's internal knowledge
frameworks that iteratively refine initial hand-crafted prompts for personalization
the user-specific subset of high-probability generations for input x whose alignment with the user's preferences passes a threshold; far smaller than S(x)
tone and style (writing style, tone), relevance (content, contextual), accuracy (factual, user data accuracy)
